output.title: Designing against eval drift starts with a threshold
output.body:
If you are automating a recurring workflow, eval drift is not abstract. It is the point where the system no longer fits the work it was built to handle. For an owner-operator, that often shows up in inbox handling, invoice review, or lead triage: the AI looked fine on the sample set, then real messages, edge cases, or a process change started to pull it off course.

The bounded decision is simple: define the workflow, the measurable outcome, and the stop rule before you automate. If the system is classifying customer emails, decide what “correct enough” means and what level of manual review triggers a pause. Any threshold is a control, not a promise.

A useful diagnostic question is: how will I know this system is drifting, and what will I do then? Human approval stays mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions. The design goal is not a silent system that hopes for the best; it is one that alerts you when patterns change and hands the decision back to you.

One practical next step is to write a single sentence for the workflow: “If X changes, we pause automation and review Y.” That turns eval drift from a vague AI concern into a clear operational boundary.
